subtype: Family member in a medical emergency [Actor]
passage:
Dear Amandeep,
On Sunday morning Amma collapsed in the kitchen. My head filled with questions at once: which hospital, who has cash, should I ring Mama first? I made myself do one thing. I dialled 112 and gave our address slowly, twice. Then I unlocked the gate, switched on the porch light and asked Mrs Rao next door to sit with Amma while I waited by the road. Only after the ambulance had left did I call the relatives, and I sorted the papers and the money on the way to the hospital. She is being looked after. I will write again tomorrow. I am tired, but I am glad I did things in that order. Karthik

qa.q: What did Karthik do first when Amma collapsed?
qa.a: Karthik dialled 112 and gave the address slowly, twice.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as the questions about hospital, cash and Mama crowded in?
qa.a: Karthik felt panicked and overwhelmed by the rush of decisions, but made an effort to do only one thing first.

qa.q: Why did Karthik leave the calls to relatives and the money questions until after the ambulance left?
qa.a: Getting help came first, and the other decisions could wait, so keeping that order stopped the panic from taking over.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt when asked to sit with Amma?
qa.a: Mrs Rao was probably worried but glad to help, since staying beside Amma gave a neighbour a clear and useful job.

passage: It was a Tuesday, in the lift lobby of our building. My father sat down on the bench and said he felt strange, and then he slumped sideways. Everything in my head started shouting: which hospital, do we have money in the account, who do I tell first? I shouted for the guard, dialled 112 and gave the block and floor. That was all I did for the first minutes, that and stay with him. Nikita, you asked what I would tell someone else. The calls to my uncle, the cash, the forms, all of that came after the ambulance. I still hear my own voice saying the address. Yamini

passage: Disha, twenty-five, was visiting her parents in their village near Hubballi when her father collapsed in the courtyard after lunch. For a second, her mind raced in every direction: which hospital, how much money was in the house, should she call her brother in Pune, her uncle, the neighbour with the jeep? Her hands trembled. Then she heard her own voice say, "First, the ambulance." She dialled 108 and gave the village name and the landmark, the Hanuman temple. Her mother held her father's hand. Only after the call did Disha ask her neighbour Noor to phone her brother. Money and the rest could wait. The ambulance came in twenty minutes.

Only when the paramedics arrived did she text her neighbour Mateo to look after the flat, and then call her brother. Paperwork could wait.

subtype: Family member in a medical emergency [Actor]
passage: In the lobby of the government office where he worked, Naveen, twenty-six, got the call from home: his mother had collapsed in the kitchen, and his younger brother Tanvir was alone with her. Naveen felt his chest tighten. He wanted to rush home, call the family doctor, think about the hospital bills and tell his aunts, all at once. He stopped himself. "Tanvir, listen. Hang up and call 108 now. Then call me back." Tanvir did. Naveen then called the neighbour to go and sit with Tanvir. Only then did he take an auto home. By the time he reached, the ambulance was there. He called his aunts from the hospital corridor.

passage:
Harsha,
You asked on the phone why you were the fifth person I called on Sunday, not the first. Here is the honest answer.
Abbu went grey and sank down right there by the tomato cart. My head filled with fifty things at once: which hospital, is there cash in my bag, where is his insurance card, should I ring you, Phuppo, Dr Qureshi? I actually had your number on the screen. Then I remembered the poster from college: call the emergency number first, everything else later. So I dialled 108. The operator asked if he was breathing, told me what to do and to stay with him. The vegetable seller held an umbrella over us. Only when the siren came did I call you, then Phuppo, then the others.
The doctors say getting him in quickly made a difference. I'm sorry you heard it fifth. I'd do it the same way again.
Hafsa

qa.a: Right there by the tomato cart.

qa.a: Hafsa was panicking, with fifty questions about the hospital, cash, the insurance card and whom to ring all crowding in at once.

qa.q: Why was dialling 108 first the right order?
qa.a: It got help moving straight away and brought the operator's instructions; calls to family and sorting out the hospital could wait until the ambulance came.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt hearing the news fifth?
